item.title: Censys Mobile DFIR Scenarios Highlight HookBot, DarkSword; Health-ISAC September Updates
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Aug 18:00 → 31 Aug 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

So Your CFO's Phone Has Been Pwned: A DFIR Journey — Optional

When a CFO’s phone is suspected of compromise, a single IOC like an IP address should be treated as the start of a broader DFIR investigation, not the incident itself. Historical infrastructure data from tools like Censys can reveal malware panels, exploit chains, related hosts, and rotating attacker infrastructure needed to scope exposure and improve detections.

  • The article presents two fictional mobile incident response scenarios involving a CFO’s phone, one using Android malware resembling ERMAC or HookBot and one involving an iPhone connection to DarkSword infrastructure.
  • In the Android scenario, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects a sideloaded malicious APK called “Chrome Update,” prompting actions such as blocking the device from corporate resources, revoking sessions, preserving the phone, and reviewing accessible credentials.
  • Censys ARC observed the Android-related host 118.107.45[.]29 carrying a HookBot threat label from mid-July through August 13, 2026, and later changes matched HookBot’s IP-whitelist security gate behavior.
  • In the iPhone scenario, Zscaler web logs show the managed iPhone connected to 103.106.190[.]217, which Censys ARC observed serving an Apple ID credential-harvesting page alongside DarkSword iOS exploit-chain infrastructure.
  • The article emphasizes that an IP address, domain, certificate, or hash is evidence of a larger infrastructure picture, and that historical Internet data can help responders scope related hosts, prior activity, and future detections.

Technologies: edr, proxy, mobile-os, browser, identity-provider, object-storage, database

item.title: Malicious Packagist Themes Deliver iOS Spyware; Varonis Warns SIEM Insufficient for Databases
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Aug 14:00 → 31 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

13 Malicious Packagist Themes Deliver iOS Spyware That Steals Crypto Wallet Seeds — Must Read

Socket researchers found 13 malicious Packagist Composer themes for Vietnamese streaming CMS sites that inject JavaScript to run ad-fraud redirects and, on vulnerable iPhones, a FUNNULL-hosted exploit chain that installs spyware. The payload can steal sensitive iOS data including keychain contents, messages, photos, location history, and crypto wallet seeds, so affected site operators should remove the packages and users should update iOS immediately.

  • Socket’s Threat Research Team found 13 malicious Composer theme packages on Packagist across five vendor namespaces that inject JavaScript into Vietnamese movie and comic streaming sites that install them.
  • The injected JavaScript runs a mobile ad-fraud and gambling-redirect chain, and on iPhones it can trigger a WebKit-to-kernel exploit chain that installs spyware.
  • Apple confirmed that the kernel escape used by the iOS chain was already fixed in iOS and macOS 26.1 before Socket’s report, while the two WebKit entry points are public and listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
  • The spyware payload can collect keychain databases, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS, address book, Photos, browser cookies, call history, location history, account databases, and crypto-wallet seed or mnemonic data from several wallet apps.
  • The article recommends that site operators remove any themes from the vsmov, vsphim, haiau009, chilltvcms, or ophimcms vendors, rotate credentials handled on the host, inspect theme scripts, and block the listed network indicators.

Technologies: package-registry, cms, mobile-os, operating-system, browser

Vendors: socket, apple, packagist, composer, ophimcms, kkphim, laravel

SIEM Is Not Enough: Why You Need DAM for Your Databases — Optional

The article argues that sending database audit logs to a SIEM is costly and lacks the data sensitivity, identity, and behavior context needed to detect real risk, especially as AI agents increase database access. It promotes Varonis Next-Gen DAM as a way to monitor all databases through native audit collection and turn raw activity into actionable security findings.

  • The article argues that sending native database audit logs to a SIEM creates high ingest costs while producing raw events that lack database security context.
  • The article says legacy agent-based DAM deployments often take years, cover only a fraction of databases, and generate many undifferentiated alerts.
  • Varonis Next-Gen DAM uses native audit collection for most major database engines and the Varonis Gatekeeper for hypercritical databases that need inline enforcement such as blocking or dynamic masking.
  • Varonis says its platform turns database activity into findings by combining data classification, identity resolution, and user behavior analytics.
  • The article highlights AI agents as a growing database security challenge because they can generate large volumes of queries through shared service accounts while obscuring the originating user or workflow.

item.title: JSCeal Deobfuscation, Next.js CVE-2026-75604, PaperCut Exploitation, and ValleyRAT Campaigns
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Aug 10:00 → 31 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-75604) Next.js Remote Code Execution via Windows Path Traversal — Should Read

A critical Next.js flaw, CVE-2026-75604, can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on self-hosted Windows deployments using affected versions and routing/cache configurations. Organizations should urgently identify Windows-hosted Next.js apps and upgrade to the fixed releases, as there is no reliable workaround.

  • CVE-2026-75604 is a critical path traversal flaw in Next.js that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to write files outside the framework’s cache directory and reach remote code execution on the host.
  • The vulnerability affects Next.js 13.4 up to 15.5.24 and 16.0 up to 16.3.3 when the application runs on a Windows filesystem and uses the Pages Router or the App Router without Cache Components.
  • Linux and macOS deployments are not affected, and applications running on Vercel’s managed platform are not affected because that infrastructure runs on Linux.
  • Vercel released fixed versions in Next.js 15.5.24 and 16.3.3, and the article states there is no known workaround for affected Windows-hosted applications.
  • The article recommends inventorying Windows-hosted Next.js deployments, confirming pinned Next.js versions, monitoring cache paths, blocking percent-encoded backslash sequences, and auditing externally reachable incremental static regeneration routes until patching is confirmed.

Technologies: operating-system, web-server

Products: next-js, cycognito-platform, windows-server, iis, libheif

Vendors: vercel, cycognito, microsoft, libheif-project

ValleyRAT masquerading as adware — Should Read

Kaspersky found that attackers are disguising the ValleyRAT backdoor as signed QN Wallpaper adware, using DLL sideloading to disable defenses, persist, steal keystrokes and clipboard data, and download additional payloads. The campaign is likely linked to Silver Fox and has mainly affected users in China and India.

  • Kaspersky analyzed an installer initially classified as adware and found that it triggered an infection chain delivering the ValleyRAT backdoor instead of functioning as advertising software.
  • The installer deployed a modified version of the Chinese QN Wallpaper desktop wallpaper tool and used a malicious libcef.dll for DLL sideloading under the guise of a signed process.
  • The malicious libcef.dll decrypted and loaded AES-encrypted ValleyRAT payloads from either the PeLoader file or its own resources, depending on whether it was running inside QnWallpaper.exe or QnwPlayer.exe.
  • ValleyRAT can log keystrokes, capture clipboard contents, collect system information, take screenshots, update C2 addresses, download additional modules, and reboot or shut down the computer on command.
  • Kaspersky detected ValleyRAT and associated malware more than 100,000 times in 2026, affecting more than 1,500 unique users primarily in China and India, and attributed the campaign as likely linked to Silver Fox.

Technologies: antivirus, operating-system

Products: qn-wallpaper, windows-defender, windows

Vendors: kaspersky, keansoft, microsoft

Breaking the Seal: Static Deobfuscation of JSCeal’s Compiled V8 Bytecode — Should Read

Check Point researchers built and released a fully static pipeline to deobfuscate JSCeal’s compiled V8 bytecode payloads, turning heavily obfuscated Node.js malware into analyzable pseudocode without executing it. The recovered code shows JSCeal is a broad crypto-focused stealer with browser credential theft, keylogging, screenshots, Telegram theft, and local HTTPS interception capabilities.

  • Check Point Research has tracked JSCeal since early 2025 as a cryptocurrency-focused stealer delivered as compiled V8 bytecode and executed by a bundled Node.js runtime.
  • The analyzed JSCeal payloads were protected with javascript-obfuscator techniques including RC4-protected strings, control-flow flattening, proxy functions, and operation wrappers.
  • Check Point Research developed and released a fully static deobfuscation toolkit that transforms View8 pseudocode without executing the malware.
  • The deobfuscated output exposed JSCeal capabilities including browser credential theft, keylogging, screenshot capture, Telegram session theft, cryptocurrency-focused collection, and HTTPS traffic interception through a local proxy.
  • More recent JSCeal developments include V8 code caches generated for a newer Node.js and V8 version, an AES-256-CBC payload-encryption layer, and macOS targeting.

Technologies: operating-system, browser, proxy

Products: jsceal, jsc-deobfuscator, view8, v8, node.js, javascript-obfuscator, brotli, puppeteer, puppeteer-extra, ghost-cursor, macos, windows

Vendors: check-point, google, nodejs, javascript-obfuscator, view8, hasherezade, microsoft

One Target List, Six Weeks of Conference Invites — Should Read

A patient phishing operator used an aged, properly authenticated attacker-owned domain to repeatedly target named employees at one pharmaceutical CDMO with personalized conference-invitation emails carrying a malicious PDF. The key lesson is that SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain age, and sender familiarity can all look normal, so defenders need payload analysis and per-recipient behavioral detection to catch these campaigns.

  • On July 9, 2026, a senior commercial leader at a pharmaceutical contract development and manufacturing organization received a personalized industry-summit invitation with a malicious brochure PDF attached.
  • Six weeks later, on August 20, 2026, four more individually named mailboxes at the same organization were targeted with similar personalized conference invitations and matching brochure attachments.
  • The emails passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication because the attacker owned and correctly configured the sending domain.
  • The attacker’s sending domain, nexora-summits[.]com, was created on December 5, 2025, making it roughly seven months old at the first recorded send.
  • The attachment scanner returned a malicious verdict on the PDF, and Themis scored the message at 90 percent confidence before mitigating it across the affected mailboxes.

Technologies: email-security

Products: themis

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft

31th August – Threat Intelligence Report — Optional

This weekly threat intelligence roundup highlights major breaches affecting airports, healthcare, and government systems, alongside emerging AI-enabled abuse and prompt-injection risks. Organizations should prioritize patching critical flaws in PaperCut, Ubiquiti, Next.js, and ServiceNow while monitoring activity from ransomware, phishing, and state-linked threat groups.

  • Manchester Airports Group disclosed a cyberattack that exposed data belonging to about 8.7 million customers, including contact details, vehicle registration numbers, and information collected through car park, lounge, fast-track, and Wi-Fi registrations.
  • McKesson disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to third-party applications and data theft, and ShinyHunters claimed it exfiltrated about 1TB of data containing approximately 284 million patient-related records.
  • Researchers described Cryptographic Context Injection, a technique that conceals malicious instructions inside encrypted content to bypass safeguards in AI assistants with browsing and code capabilities.
  • PaperCut released emergency fixes for two actively exploited vulnerabilities affecting PaperCut NG and MF that attackers can chain to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on affected servers.
  • U.S. authorities announced the disruption of QScan and QTRouter, two platforms operated by the China-linked group QTFY to target U.S. critical infrastructure and government networks.

item.title: Microsoft Quarantine Release Delivered DMARC-Reject Spoofed Invoice Email
item.content:encoded:
Window: 30 Aug 10:00 → 30 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

DMARC Said Reject. A Quarantine Release Delivered It Anyway — May Read

A spoofed QuickBooks-style invoice email that failed SPF, had no DKIM, and failed DMARC under a reject policy was correctly quarantined by Microsoft but later delivered after being resubmitted from quarantine by an internal account. The key risk is that quarantine release can undo strong authentication enforcement, especially for payload-free invoice fraud that relies only on getting a victim to reply.

  • A spoofed accounting-brand invoice notice reached a shared accounts-payable mailbox at a financial-advisory firm after Microsoft’s antispam engine had quarantined it on August 13, 2026.
  • The original authentication results showed SPF failed for sending IP 209[.]222[.]82[.]241, DKIM was absent, and DMARC failed against a domain publishing an enforced reject policy.
  • Headers on the delivered copy showed it was resubmitted out of quarantine, including an Exchange generated-message-source value of Antispam Quarantine Agent, Auto-Submitted: auto-generated, and X-MS-Exchange-QuarantineResubmitTime.
  • The release was attributed in headers to an internal mailbox, but the article says the headers do not show whether it was an end-user self-service release or an administrator action.
  • The message contained no attachment, link, or embedded image, and its only attack surface was the reply address accounts@ap2-linkedin[.]com on a privacy-protected domain created on April 16, 2026.

Technologies: email-security

Products: microsoft-exchange, quickbooks, adaptive-ai

Vendors: microsoft, intuit, ironscales, dynadot

item.title: CyCognito Frames Attack Surface Management as Change Management Discipline
item.content:encoded:
Window: 30 Aug 06:00 → 30 Aug 10:00 UTC (4 hours)

ASM Has a Silent C, and It Stands for Change Management — Optional

The article argues that attack surface management should be treated as continuous change management, not just vulnerability tracking, because AI-driven self-service infrastructure is making assets and misconfigurations appear faster. Effective ASM needs frequent discovery, business context, change-aware prioritization, deeper validation, and proof that fixes actually worked.

  • The article argues that attack surface management should be viewed as a change management function rather than only as support for vulnerability management.
  • The author says the time between a misconfiguration going live and an attacker finding it is shrinking, while such gaps are appearing more often because more people can deploy to production with AI-assisted self-service infrastructure.
  • The article states that an attack surface should be treated as a graph of related assets and dependencies, not simply as a list of assets.
  • The author says daily discovery has become a baseline expectation, citing a 2025 SANS survey in which 59% of respondents preferred daily scan frequency.
  • The article says remediation should include re-validating fixes because roughly 25% of issues marked resolved still leave the underlying risk open.

Products: target-graph

Vendors: cycognito, sans

item.title: Malicious npm Releases Hit @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen via GitHub Actions Trusted Publishing
item.content:encoded:
Window: 29 Aug 14:00 → 29 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Mini Shai-Hulud hits openapi-react-query-codegen: 10 malicious npm versions — Must Read

Ten malicious versions of @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen were published to npm after an attacker abused a GitHub Actions issue_comment release workflow to mint trusted publishing tokens without stealing maintainer credentials. Some versions executed without install scripts via node-gyp, so affected users must check for the listed versions and payload files, update to a clean release, and rotate exposed credentials.

  • On August 28, 2026, ten malicious versions of @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen were published to npm between 20:00 and 20:21 UTC, with the latest tag pointing to malicious version 3.0.4 during that window.
  • The attacker abused a GitHub Actions release workflow triggered by issue_comment events that checked out pull request code and had id-token: write permission, allowing npm trusted publishing tokens to be minted without a stolen npm token or hijacked maintainer account.
  • Eight of the malicious releases contained a multi-stage loader that targeted cloud, registry, and developer credentials, while two prerelease versions used a preinstall script but did not include the payload files.
  • Four affected versions had no install script and executed through node-gyp evaluation of a malicious binding.gyp file, so scanning only for install hooks would miss them.
  • The article recommends auditing lockfiles and install logs for the ten affected versions, updating to a clean version, rotating credentials reachable from affected machines or runners, and reviewing AI assistant configuration files for unexpected changes.

Technologies: package-registry, ci-cd, source-control

Products: openapi-react-query-codegen, npm, github-actions, npm-trusted-publishing, node-gyp, bun, react-query

Vendors: 7nohe, npm, github, nodejs, oven-sh, mend-io

item.title: Google Forms Credential Theft Lure Sent From Compromised Legacy Business Domain
item.content:encoded:
Window: 29 Aug 10:00 → 29 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Nothing to Block: A 1990s Domain and a Google Form — Should Read

A phishing email sent from a compromised, decades-old legitimate mailbox passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC and used a Google Forms link for credential harvesting, leaving no obvious reputation-based indicators to block. The key takeaway is that clean authentication and trusted hosting do not prove an email is safe; detection must evaluate message content, sender relationship, and behavior.

  • A general manager at a national in-home care services provider received an unbranded payment notice from a legitimate property-management business domain registered in the late 1990s.
  • The email passed DKIM, SPF, and DMARC because it was sent from a real compromised mailbox rather than from spoofed infrastructure.
  • The single hyperlink in the message was a Google Forms shortlink that redirected to a form page on Google's own document platform.
  • The lure used fabricated transaction details, including a customer identifier, paid date, BILLPAY memo, and reference number, while omitting the payment amount and showing a mismatch between the subject and body reference numbers.
  • IRONSCALES' Themis Adaptive AI classified the message as credential theft at 83 percent confidence based on content and behavior rather than infrastructure reputation signals.

Technologies: email-security, cloud-platform

Products: google-forms, google-docs, themis, ironscales-adaptive-ai

Vendors: google, ironscales

item.title: OpenAPI React Query Codegen npm worm, HexMage Magecart, NetSupport fake MP4 campaigns
item.content:encoded:
Window: 28 Aug 18:00 → 28 Aug 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

Popular code generator for TanStack Query hit by supply chain worm — Must Read

A popular npm package, @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen, was compromised with a supply-chain worm that runs during install via a binding.gyp/node-gyp sandbox escape. The malware steals developer, cloud, CI/CD, and local credentials and affected multiple published package versions.

  • Aikido detected TeamPCP-like malware in the npm package @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen, which has more than 150,000 weekly downloads and generates type-safe TanStack Query hooks from an OpenAPI schema.
  • The malware executes during npm install through a binding.gyp file that abuses node-gyp’s Python condition evaluation to run node 3FWCvzduYZg.js without a preinstall script in package.json.
  • The payload, which calls itself “Trinitite: Sponsored by Preview 2 Effects,” uses multiple layers of encryption and obfuscation and includes a credential harvester, a worm, and a destructive command.
  • Before running, the payload exits silently under several conditions, including Russian locale settings, certain endpoint security directories, known security-scanner environments, selected GitHub repository owners, and StepSecurity harden-runner activity.
  • The malware targets GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, AWS, Azure, GCP, HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes, SSH keys, Docker credentials, environment files, crypto wallets, messaging session data, VPN configs, Claude AI files, and JFrog Artifactory tokens.

Technologies: package-registry, ci-cd, source-control, cloud-platform, secrets-manager, orchestration, container-platform

Products: openapi-react-query-codegen, npm, tanstack-query, node-gyp, node.js, bun, github-actions, github, amazon-ec2, amazon-ecs, aws-sts, azure-key-vault, azure-resource-manager, microsoft-graph, google-secret-manager, hashicorp-vault, kubernetes

Vendors: 7nohe, npm, tanstack, nodejs, bun, github, amazon-web-services, microsoft, google-cloud, hashicorp, kubernetes

Skimming on the Blockchain: A Magecart Campaign That Uses EtherHiding, Found by Malvertising Scanning — Must Read

Confiant uncovered a Magecart campaign called HexMage that compromises e-commerce checkouts and uses Ethereum Sepolia smart contracts as resilient staging to deliver card skimmers from rotating domains. The key takeaway is that EtherHiding has moved beyond fake-update malware into payment-card theft, with one wallet-linked infrastructure spanning dozens of merchant sites and hundreds of contracts.

  • Confiant tracks this Magecart card-skimming campaign as HexMage, and it was detected through malvertising scanning of ads run by compromised merchants.
  • The attackers compromise legitimate e-commerce storefronts, mostly WooCommerce sites, and inject a small server-side loader disguised as a Google Tag Manager code block.
  • The loader usually pulls ethers.js and reads an attacker-controlled smart contract on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet to retrieve a disposable skimmer delivery domain.
  • The skimmer overlays or replaces payment forms, steals cardholder data and billing details, exfiltrates them in base64-encoded requests, and then restores the page so the purchase appears to complete normally.
  • Confiant analyzed 25 victim storefronts, 20 Sepolia contracts, and 20 skimmer-hosting domains, and found the contracts shared a single owner wallet that had deployed 144 such contracts since March 2026.

Technologies: cms

Products: ethereum, sepolia, ethers-js, google-tag-manager, jsdelivr, 0xrpc, woocommerce, wordpress, prestashop, magento, stripe-elements

Vendors: confiant, ethereum, google, jsdelivr, 0xrpc, automattic, wordpress, prestashop, adobe, stripe

The Video That Plays You: Fake MP4 File Carries Malicious Payload — Should Read

Censys found a malware delivery chain that disguises an encrypted PowerShell payload inside a fake, non-playable MP4 file, which ultimately installs a silent NetSupport Manager client for remote access. The campaign uses rotating Cloudflare-fronted delivery hosts, MP4 carrier files, and C2 gateways to evade basic detection and maintain control of infected systems.

  • Censys ARC observed a Cloudflare-fronted host serving raw PowerShell over port 80 on 22 August 2026.
  • The delivery chain uses a PowerShell loader to retrieve a fake MP4 file that contains 6.5 MB of encrypted NetSupport client data in an ISO Base Media File Format uuid extension box.

Securing Docker images — Optional

Securing Docker images is an ongoing vulnerability management process: use minimal hardened bases, remove unused packages, run with least privilege, keep secrets out of layers, pin carefully, and continuously rebuild or patch as new flaws appear. The article argues that patched drop-in replacements for the same base image versions can reduce risk without forcing disruptive distro or version migrations.

  • Most container vulnerabilities come from the open source packages and libraries included in the base image, including components the application may never use.
  • Deleting a file or package in a later Docker layer only hides it, because earlier layers remain immutable and can still contain what the base image shipped.
  • Securing Docker images involves shrinking the attack surface, setting permissions correctly, keeping secrets out of image layers, pinning base images carefully, and continuously re-checking images for new vulnerabilities.
  • A hardened image can become vulnerable over time because new vulnerabilities are disclosed against packages that are already inside it.
  • Aikido provides patched builds of the same base image versions teams already run, delivered as pull requests, so they can stay on tested versions while applying fixes.
